questions.q: It memorises one batch, but the full run is still flat. Now what?
questions.a: The code can learn, so check the usual causes: the learning rate (try 0.1, 0.01, 0.001), starting weights, and the data. Karpathy's recipe says to look at exactly what enters the network, “immediately before your y_hat = model(x)”.

teach.title: How it works: four steps, in order

questions.q: Can passing the one-batch test still hide a bug?
questions.a: Yes: it only shows the model can learn something. Karpathy's example of a silent bug (our link to the one-batch test) is an off-by-one bug that lets an autoregressive model, which predicts each next token from earlier ones, see the token it should predict, so (our inference) the loss falls too well. Check the inputs and labels too.

teach.title: How it works: four steps, in order

questions.q: Why switch off dropout for the test?
questions.a: Dropout randomly zeroes units on every training pass, which fights memorising. Karpathy's recipe turns off data augmentation (random changes to training examples, such as flips or crops) at this stage for the same kind of reason; dropout is our addition. A failure then points at the code, not at noise.

teach.title: How it works: four steps, in order

questions.q: A language model has a 32,000-token vocabulary. What should its loss be at step zero?
questions.a: About ln 32,000 ≈ 10.4, the loss of an even guess over every token. That is Karpathy's −log(1/n_classes) check.

teach.title: How it works: four steps, in order

questions.q: Why overfit a single small batch before tuning anything?
questions.a: A working model can memorise a few examples. If it can't drive that loss near zero, the code has a bug, and no learning rate or optimizer will fix it.

questions.q: One layer's gradient is exactly zero at every step. What does that tell you?
questions.a: The loss never reaches that layer, so its weights never change: something cuts the chain (a detach, an unused output) or its ReLU units are dead.
